sources.title: WHO guideline for non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain in adults in primary and community care settings
sources.population: Adults including older adults with chronic primary low-back pain in primary/community care
sources.findings: WHO, 2023 final guideline. Official publication; recommendations; ISBN 9789240081789. FT relevant exercise recommendation. Adults including older adults, chronic primary LBP in primary/community care; specific causes require separate assessment. Structured exercise may be offered as part of care (conditional; low certainty). Individualization, preferences, capacity and access matter; a single preferred exercise modality or universal load/ROM ceiling is not established. Evidence includes temporary symptom exacerbation; harms are incompletely captured. This is a treatment recommendation, not evidence that every gym execution is appropriate.
sources.limitations: Conditional recommendation; low certainty; no preferred universal exercise modality Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Systematic Review to Inform a World Health Organization (WHO) Clinical Practice Guideline: Benefits and Harms of Structured Exercise Programs for Chronic Primary Low Back Pain in Adults.
sources.population: Adults with chronic primary low-back pain; two trials included adults aged at least 60
sources.findings: Verville et al., 2023, WHO exercise systematic review. DOI 10.1007/s10926-023-10124-4, PMID 37991647, PMC10684665. FT. Search updated through May 2022; primary analysis 13 low/unclear-risk RCTs, 1362 adults; two trials included adults ≥60. Aerobic, strengthening, mixed, Pilates, flexibility, yoga and motor-control programs versus no intervention/usual care/sham. Benefits vary by modality, comparator and time; certainty for individual modalities low/very low. Harms sparse, mainly temporary pain increases. Supports an exercise category with individual selection; not an exact sequence or exclusion list.
sources.limitations: Individual modality evidence low/very low certainty; pooled categories do not identify exact executions Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Exercise therapy for chronic low back pain.
sources.population: Chronic nonspecific low-back pain lasting over 12 weeks
sources.findings: Hayden et al., 2021 Cochrane review. DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD009790.pub2, PMID 34580864, PMC8477273. Abstract and publisher conclusions inspected; not all underlying trials. 249 RCTs, 24,486 participants, chronic nonspecific LBP >12 weeks. Earliest follow-up: exercise versus no treatment/usual care/placebo reduced pain 15.2/100 (95% CI 12.2–18.3), functional limitation 6.8/100 (5.3–8.3); functional difference below review's clinical-importance threshold. Heterogeneity and trial bias matter. Adverse reporting insufficient to establish comprehensive safety; reported events mostly minor muscle pain. No evidence here for a blanket spinal flexion, rotation, squat or lifting ban.
sources.limitations: Heterogeneity and trial bias; functional effect below review clinical-importance threshold Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Individualized low-load motor control exercises and education versus a high-load lifting exercise and education to improve activity, pain intensity, and physical performance in patients with low back pain: a randomized controlled trial.
sources.population: Recurrent mechanical/nociceptive-dominant low-back pain
sources.findings: Aasa et al., 2015 RCT. DOI 10.2519/jospt.2015.5021, PMID 25641309. Abstract. 70 adults with recurrent mechanical/nociceptive-dominant LBP; low-load motor control versus high-load lifting, both education; 12 sessions/8 weeks. Motor control improved patient-specific activity more (4.2 versus 2.5 points); no significant between-group pain difference. Does not establish lifting as universally unsafe or equivalent for every chronic-primary-LBP phenotype. Detailed adverse/progression data taken from its same-cohort follow-up below, not invented from abstract.
sources.limitations: Activity favored low-load intervention; pain between-group difference nonsignificant; not independent of LBP-P2 Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: High load lifting exercise and low load motor control exercises as interventions for patients with mechanical low back pain: A randomized controlled trial with 24-month follow-up.
sources.population: Mechanical nociceptive-dominant low-back pain over three months; primarily ages 25–60; nerve-root compression/acute disc herniation and specific pathology excluded
sources.findings: Michaelson et al., 2016 same-cohort RCT follow-up. DOI 10.2340/16501977-2091, journal full text PDF. FT. 35/group; mechanical LBP >3 months; 8-week intervention, 2-,12-,24-month outcomes. No significant between-group pain/disability/QoL differences; no untreated control. Deadlift progression was supervised and contingent on pain before/during/after; no 1RM testing. Two high-load participants reported adverse effects, one withdrew; none reported in low-load arm. Selected population and close technique/progression supervision limit unsupervised generalization. Supports individualized progression and a lower-load alternative; not a rule that all patients must avoid deadlifts or remain neutral in every daily movement.
sources.limitations: No untreated control; close supervision and selected phenotype limit app transfer Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Management of low back pain and lumbosacral radicular syndrome: the Guideline of the Royal Dutch Society for Physical Therapy (KNGF).
sources.population: Adults with low-back pain/lumbosacral radicular syndrome without red flags; severe neurological presentations/recent surgery outside scope
sources.findings: Apeldoorn et al., KNGF guideline, 2024 final. DOI 10.23736/S1973-9087.24.08352-7, PMID 38407016, PMC11112513; FT via Europe PMC XML. Adults LBP/lumbosacral radicular syndrome without red flags. Activity/exercise progression depends pain/irritability: avoid increasing pain in high irritability; brief increase may be acceptable in moderate irritability. This is individualized guidance, not a fixed joint angle cap. Immediate physician contact advised for saddle numbness, bowel/bladder changes or increasing leg weakness. Severe neurological cases and recent surgery fall outside guideline scope; that scope limit is not itself a trial-proven contraindication. No universal flexion/extension or lifting exclusion established.
sources.limitations: Irritability-specific guidance requires assessment; scope exclusions are not proof of universal exercise harm Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Physical Therapy Referral From Primary Care for Acute Back Pain With Sciatica : A Randomized Controlled Trial.
sources.population: Ages 18–60, recent sciatica under 90 days
sources.findings: Fritz et al., 2021 (online 2020) pragmatic RCT. DOI 10.7326/M20-4187, PMID 33017565, PMC7856080. FT. 220 adults 18–60, recent sciatica <90 days. Education versus education plus 4-week PT including individualized directional exercise/manual therapy (recommended 6–8 visits; home exercise every 4–5 hours). Disability advantage at 6 months −5.4/100 (95% CI −9.4 to −1.3); at one year −4.8 (−8.9 to −0.7); no health-care-use/work-loss difference. Thirty-seven PT recipients reported 133 effects, commonly back pain/stiffness; 13 effects severe in intensity, seven persisted >24 h. Movements chosen to centralize symptoms; extension often used, never automatically for all. Cannot isolate exercise from manual therapy or establish an unsupervised gym prescription.
sources.limitations: Package effects cannot isolate exercise; directional response assessed clinically Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Physical therapy plus general practitioners' care versus general practitioners' care alone for sciatica: a randomised clinical trial with a 12-month follow-up.
sources.population: Acute sciatica in general practice
sources.findings: Luijsterburg et al., 2008 RCT. DOI 10.1007/s00586-007-0569-6, PMID 18172697, PMC2295266. Abstract/available summary; FT not yet extracted. Acute sciatica, GP care with versus without added PT, 12-month follow-up. Added PT improved global perceived recovery at 12 months, without significant relevant differences in leg pain, disability, fear or general health; not more cost effective. Included as contrary/qualified evidence: PT benefits depend on outcome and care package, and do not prove particular ordinary exercises harmful. Dose/adverse details unresolved here.
sources.limitations: Global recovery improved, without relevant significant differences in leg pain/disability/fear/general health; cost effectiveness not improved Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: The Effectiveness and Optimal Dose of Resistance Training in Patients With Subacute and Persistent Low Back-Related Leg Pain: A Systematic Review.
sources.population: Mixed low-back-related leg pain including referred pain; 212 recruited in body versus 196 analyzed in abstract
sources.findings: Barbari et al., 2024 systematic review. DOI 10.7759/cureus.57278, PMID 38559546, PMC10981532; FT via XML. Two resistance-training RCTs; abstract reports 196 analyzed participants, body 212 recruited. Mixed low-back-related leg pain, including referred pain, not a homogeneous confirmed radiculopathy cohort. One versus two sets showed no clear difference; individual functional restoration versus advice yielded limited/mixed superiority. No serious adverse events reported; optimal dose/long-term superiority uncertain. Cannot turn these mixed-population findings into radiculopathy-specific load ceilings or assume neural “flossing” is equivalent to strength training.
sources.limitations: Not a homogeneous confirmed radiculopathy cohort; optimal dose uncertain Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Saudi Clinical Practice Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Low Back Pain and Sciatica in Adults.
sources.population: Adults with nonspecific low-back pain/sciatica, Saudi health-system context
sources.findings: Aldera et al., 2026 final Saudi adapted guideline. DOI 10.3390/jcm15020528, PMID 41598467, PMC12842004; selected FT sections via XML. Adults nonspecific LBP/sciatica in Saudi health-system context. Psychological care suggested as part of an exercise-containing package; low/very-low certainty predominates. The inspected sections do not establish execution-level bans. Not used to invent new workout rules; full module-by-module extraction remains a gap.
sources.limitations: Selected sections only; generally low/very-low certainty; not execution-specific evidence Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Non-Surgical Interventions for Lumbar Spinal Stenosis Leading To Neurogenic Claudication: A Clinical Practice Guideline.
sources.population: Adults with lumbar spinal stenosis causing neurogenic claudication
sources.findings: Bussières et al., 2021 final clinical practice guideline. DOI 10.1016/j.jpain.2021.03.147, author-institution PDF. Relevant final recommendation text inspected. Adults LSS causing neurogenic claudication. Conditional/weak recommendation for multimodal nonpharmacologic care: education/advice, behavioral change, home exercise, manual therapy/rehabilitation (moderate-quality evidence). Postoperative rehabilitation is a separate setting/timing. Does not prescribe one universal flexion dose or ban all extension/standing. NASS official completed-guideline page inspected: LSS guideline remains listed under 2011, not 2025 (the nearby 2025 header belongs to antithrombotics).
sources.limitations: Weak/conditional recommendation; postoperative rehabilitation is separate; no uniform flexion regimen Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Exercise treatments for lumbar spinal stenosis: A systematic review and intervention component analysis of randomised controlled trials.
sources.population: Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication
sources.findings: Comer et al., 2024 (online 2023) systematic review/component analysis. DOI 10.1177/02692155231201048, PMID 37715644, PMC10829420; FT via XML. Thirteen trials, 1440 participants with neurogenic claudication; 23 exercise interventions, heterogeneous comparators. Supervision/flexion common; cycling, strengthening, stretching and psychological components more frequent in successful packages. Flexion itself appeared in both successful and unsuccessful programs. Component co-occurrence is not randomized proof of independent benefit or safety; no reliable supervision/dose conclusion. Supports considering tolerable fitness/strengthening within a multimodal plan, not prohibiting all extension or inferring every stretch is beneficial.
sources.limitations: Component co-occurrence does not identify causal effect; flexion occurs in successful and unsuccessful packages Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Comparative Clinical Effectiveness of Nonsurgical Treatment Methods in Patients With Lumbar Spinal Stenosis: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
sources.population: Adults at least 60, imaging-confirmed stenosis and neurogenic claudication; excluded cauda equina/prior stenosis surgery or fusion/severe competing walking conditions
sources.findings: Schneider et al., 2019 RCT. DOI 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2018.6828, journal FT. FT. 259 adults ≥60, imaging-confirmed LSS and neurogenic claudication; symptoms relieved by sitting/flexion among diagnostic signs. Six-week medical care, group exercise or manual therapy/individualized exercise; outcomes 2/6 months. Individualized package improved symptom/function scores more at 2 months; no between-group responder differences at 6 months. All groups improved walking. No serious treatment-related events; transient muscle soreness 54% individualized, 31% group exercise, 6% medical; all anticipated events resolved ≤48h. Excluded cauda equina, prior stenosis surgery/fusion and severe competing walking conditions; exclusions limit generalization. Symptom relief supports a tolerability-based posture adaptation, not proof extension damages tissue.
sources.limitations: Short-term between-group benefit did not persist at six months; package effects; diagnostic relief with sitting/flexion is not tissue-harm evidence Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: A home exercise programme is no more beneficial than advice and education for people with neurogenic claudication: results from a randomised controlled trial.
sources.population: Adults at least 50 with walking-limited neurogenic claudication
sources.findings: Comer et al., 2013 RCT. DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0072878, PMID 24098633, journal FT. FT available text. Adults ≥50 with walking-limited neurogenic claudication; six-week home flexion/aerobic exercise plus advice versus advice/education. No significant symptom-severity benefit at 8 weeks (adjusted difference 0.06; 95% CI −0.19 to 0.31); no systematic sustained improvement; 12-month outcomes measured. No adverse events reported. Mean three contacts; post hoc severe-symptom subgroup not confirmatory. Important contrary evidence against claiming an app-delivered generic flexion program will reproduce supervised rehabilitation benefits.
sources.limitations: No significant primary benefit; severe-subgroup post hoc finding not confirmatory Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: A comparison between two physical therapy treatment programs for patients with lumbar spinal stenosis: a randomized clinical trial.
sources.population: Lumbar spinal stenosis
sources.findings: Whitman et al., 2006 RCT. DOI 10.1097/01.brs.0000241136.98159.8c, PMID 17047542. Abstract; full PDF located but not fully extracted. 58 people LSS, six-week manual therapy/body-weight-supported walking/exercise versus flexion/walking/subtherapeutic ultrasound. Recovery better with manual/exercise package (NNT 2.6 at six weeks); 62% versus 41% recovered at one year. Multi-component comparison cannot identify which exercise determines benefit, dose, or contraindications. Detailed harms unresolved.
sources.limitations: Multicomponent contrast; no independent exercise-effect or contraindication inference Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Clinical Practice Guideline: Nonspecific Neck Pain.
sources.population: Adults with nonspecific neck pain; chronic over 12 weeks for exercise recommendation
sources.findings: El-Allawy et al., 2025 final German S3 guideline summary. DOI 10.3238/arztebl.m2025.0119, PMID 40665902, FT PMC12620902; official guideline, published August 2025, valid to February 2030. FT summary. Adults without identified structural cause; exercise recommended for chronic >12-week pain, activation/self-management central. Specific exercise modality not established because interventions heterogeneous. Immobilization discouraged; neurological deficit/trauma or structural warning signs require evaluation. No exercise dose, overhead lifting cap or cervical ROM prohibition established. Summary explicitly says these consensus-evaluated S3 guidelines are not separately journal peer reviewed; preserve distinction from peer-reviewed primary studies.
sources.limitations: Heterogeneous interventions prevent selecting a single modality/dose; structural warning signs need evaluation Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Resistance, Motor Control, and Mindfulness-Based Exercises Are Effective for Treating Chronic Nonspecific Neck Pain: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis and Dose-Response Meta-Regression.
sources.population: Adults with chronic nonspecific neck pain
sources.findings: Mueller et al., 2023 systematic review/meta-analysis. DOI 10.2519/jospt.2023.11820, PMID 37339388. Abstract and publisher results text. 68 trials chronic nonspecific neck pain; resistance, motor-control and mindfulness-based exercise versus controls/other exercises. Benefit for pain/disability, very-low to moderate certainty; substantial heterogeneity (many I² values >90%). No resistance-exercise dose-response relationship demonstrated. Modality rankings do not prove alternatives dangerous or provide safe loads for individual users. Full protocol and harms extraction remains incomplete.
sources.limitations: Very low to moderate certainty; substantial heterogeneity, many I-squared values above 90%; resistance dose-response not demonstrated Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Active neck muscle training in the treatment of chronic neck pain in women: a randomized controlled trial.
sources.population: Female office workers ages 25–53, neck pain over six months; excluded severe cervical structural/traumatic/postoperative disease and major competing conditions
sources.findings: Ylinen et al., 2003 RCT. DOI 10.1001/jama.289.19.2509, PMID 12759322, journal FT. FT. 180 female office workers with chronic nonspecific neck pain. Twelve-month isometric strength/dynamic endurance programs versus stretching/aerobic advice; supervised introductory rehabilitation then home practice encouraged three times weekly. Both active programs reduced pain/disability more; included upper-body dumbbell presses, rows and shrugs as part of package. Excluded major structural/radicular/traumatic/postoperative disease. Systematic adverse-event reporting not identified. Selected supervised population and mixed package prevent assuming every press/shrug is safe for every neck disorder; equally, findings undermine an evidence-free diagnosis-wide ban on all upper-body resistance work.
sources.limitations: Selected working women; multimodal package; no automatic transfer to cervical radicular pain or WAD Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Cervicaal Radiculair Syndroom: Oefentherapie
sources.population: Cervical radicular syndrome; assessment and stage-specific care
sources.findings: Dutch NVvN cervical radicular syndrome guideline, final July 24, 2024. Exercise module. FT module. Consider targeted exercise with a suitably experienced therapist; low-certainty pain/disability evidence, very-low/absent evidence for several outcomes/harms. Initial reactive phase prioritizes advice to avoid aggravation; subacute active approach respects individual capacity; later self-management. This clinical stage advice does not yield a fixed extension/rotation or lifting ban. Evidence synthesis finds little/no additional disability benefit over wait-and-see or other exercise. Unknown stage should not become an invented “approved” neck-strengthening routine.
sources.limitations: Stage and capacity advice is clinical guidance, not fixed extension/rotation/load limits Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Cervical collar or physiotherapy versus wait and see policy for recent onset cervical radiculopathy: randomised trial.
sources.population: Cervical radiculopathy onset under one month
sources.findings: Kuijper et al., 2009 RCT. DOI 10.1136/bmj.b3883, BMJ full article. Substantive full article text available in search result; direct open subsequently 403. 205 recent-onset (<1 month) cervical radiculopathy patients; collar/rest, PT/home exercises, or wait-and-see; six-week treatment, six-month follow-up. Hands-off graded mobilizing/stabilizing/strengthening PT twice weekly. Arm/neck pain reduction over six weeks favored collar or PT (~12–17 mm/100 difference); little/no persistent between-group difference by six months. Adverse-event outcome absent per CR-G1's synthesis. Collar/rest arm's short-term efficacy does not justify app-imposed immobilization, especially when applying a different neck-pain diagnosis or recovery stage.
sources.limitations: Direct BMJ fetch 403 after indexed substantive article text; conservative abstract-only serialization; short-term pain benefit did not establish persistent superiority Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: The Effects of Neck-Specific Training Versus Prescribed Physical Activity on Pain and Disability in Patients With Cervical Radiculopathy: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
sources.population: Confirmed cervical radiculopathy
sources.findings: Dedering et al., 2018 RCT. DOI 10.1016/j.apmr.2018.06.008, PMID 30473018. Abstract; protocol details additionally inspected in CR-G1 and CR-S1, not primary FT. 144 confirmed CR patients; three-month neck-specific training versus prescribed general physical activity; both behavioral approach, outcomes 3/6/12/24 months. No significant group or group×time effects; both improved. Guideline describes progression from gentle isometrics to low-load endurance, response-tailored, three sessions/week; comparator aerobic/muscular activity ~30 min three times/week. Primary detailed harms unavailable. Supports several possible active pathways, not superiority of one specific execution or a blanket general-activity ban.
sources.limitations: No significant overall group/group-by-time effects; secondary review contrasts should not be described as decisive superiority Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Effectiveness of Multimodal Rehabilitation Interventions for Management of Cervical Radiculopathy in Adults: An Updated Systematic Review from the Ontario Protocol for Traffic Injury Management (Optima) Collaboration.
sources.population: Adults with recent/any-duration cervical radiculopathy
sources.findings: Mallard et al., 2022 updated OPTIMa review. DOI 10.2340/jrm.v54.2799, PMID 35797062, FT PMC9422871. FT relevant synthesis. Four acceptable RCTs and one low-quality RCT, adults recent/any-duration radiculopathy; multimodal rehabilitation compared with traction, general activity, injection or surgery-containing care. Benefits generally small/trivial and low certainty; safety evidence lacking. Review's short-term pairwise signal favoring multimodal rehabilitation is compatible with the original trial's nonsignificant overall group/time model; do not present as decisive superiority.
sources.limitations: Small/trivial benefits, low certainty; heterogeneous care packages Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: What components and formats of rehabilitation interventions are more effective to reduce pain in patients with cervical radiculopathy? A Systematic review and component network meta-analysis.
sources.population: Patients with cervical radiculopathy
sources.findings: Núñez de Arenas-Arroyo et al., 2025 component network meta-analysis. DOI 10.1177/02692155251365193, publisher abstract. Abstract. Search to July 1, 2025; 36 RCTs, 25 interventions, eight active components. Neurodynamic/articular/traction-containing combinations and strengthening appeared promising for pain, moderate confidence for selected combinations. Component network assumptions, heterogeneous packages and short-term pain focus do not establish exercise contraindications or permit self-directed traction/manipulation/dry needling. Detailed adverse-event and dose extraction unavailable.
sources.limitations: Network assumptions/heterogeneity; selected moderate-confidence combinations do not prove execution safety or contraindications Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Guidelines for the management of acute whiplash-associated disorders – for health professionals. Third edition 2014.
sources.population: Adults in first 12 weeks after whiplash, with assessed WAD
sources.findings: SIRA, final third edition 2014 acute WAD guideline. Official landing page, updated Dec 19 2024; final PDF. FT relevant sections/appendix. Adults first 12 weeks; advises activity and neck ROM/low-load isometric/postural endurance/strengthening exercise. Appendix cautions exercises should not cause severe pain and higher strengthening examples start later in recovery with treating-professional guidance. Example holds are source-specific, not generic five-second progression. Online fourth-edition document explicitly titled Draft; not adopted here as current final guidance. No diagnosis-wide lifelong lifting or movement prohibition.
sources.limitations: Fourth-edition document located as Draft, not substituted for final; later recovery strengthening needs treating-professional judgment Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: The effect of neck-specific exercise with, or without a behavioral approach, on pain, disability, and self-efficacy in chronic whiplash-associated disorders: a randomized clinical trial.
sources.population: Chronic WAD grades II and III
sources.findings: Ludvigsson et al., 2015 RCT (online 2014). DOI 10.1097/AJP.0000000000000123, PMID 24918474, PMC4352069; FT via XML. 216 adults chronic WAD grades II/III. Twelve weeks neck-specific exercise (NSE), NSE plus behavioral approach, or prescribed general activity; two supervised visits/week plus home exercise. NSE progressed gentle isometrics to resistance/endurance, symptom/capacity tailored. NSE arms had greater disability improvement at 3/6 months; no significant difference between NSE arms. One arm avoided pain aggravation; behavioral arm deemphasized temporary increases. Adverse-event section not found. Thus no evidence for one universal zero-pain rule, mandatory grade-III exclusion, or unrestricted pain-pushing; clinician monitoring is material.
sources.limitations: NSE arms improved disability more; no significant differences between NSE arms; pain-response approaches differed Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Comprehensive physiotherapy exercise programme or advice for chronic whiplash (PROMISE): a pragmatic randomised controlled trial.
sources.population: Ages 18–65, chronic WAD grades I/II, 3 months–5 years; excluded nerve-root compromise
sources.findings: Michaleff et al., 2014 PROMISE RCT. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(14)60457-8, full article PDF mirror. FT. 172 adults 18–65, WAD I/II, 3 months–5 years; comprehensive 20-session PT exercise versus one advice session/phone support. At 14 weeks pain difference 0.0/10 (95% CI −0.7 to 0.7); no advantage at 6/12 months. No serious adverse events recorded. Nerve-root compromise/grade III excluded, limiting scope; not proof grade III exercise is unsafe (WAD-P1 studied it). Contrary evidence prevents promising that more sessions or complexity necessarily improves outcomes.
sources.limitations: Primary pain difference zero at 14 weeks; intensive package not superior; grade III exclusion is applicability boundary Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Pain Science Education, Stress Management, and Cognition-Targeted Exercise Therapy in Chronic Whiplash Disorders: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
sources.population: Ages 18–65, chronic WAD
sources.findings: Malfliet et al., 2025 RCT. DOI 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.26674, PMID 40794407, PMC12344539. Abstract and relevant results/full PDF excerpts. 120 adults 18–65 chronic WAD; pain-science/stress-management/cognition-targeted exercise versus usual physiotherapy. Prespecified six-month disability endpoint negative (difference 2.38/50; 95% CI −0.12 to 4.89); secondary immediate/12-month differences favored intervention. Other pain/QoL differences absent. Full harms/dose not extracted; cannot use this to mandate a universal pain-response progression model.
sources.limitations: Primary six-month disability difference nonsignificant; secondary endpoints favored intervention; full dose/harms not extracted Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: The Effect of Neck-Specific Exercise with or Without a Behavioral Approach in Chronic Whiplash-Associated Disorders: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
sources.population: Chronic WAD adults ages 18–63 in included reports
sources.findings: Correia et al., 2025 systematic review/meta-analysis. DOI 10.3390/muscles4040049, PMID 41283437, PMC12641875. Abstract only; PMC challenge/MDPI rate-limit prevented FT. Thirteen reports, 2427 participants 18–63, neck-specific exercise ± behavioral approach; quantitative pooling found no clear between-approach pain/disability advantage at follow-up despite some individual positive reports. Need check overlapping cohorts before treating participant total as independent unique patients. Does not establish acute WAD advice or a prohibition against ordinary exercise; harms/dose unresolved.
sources.limitations: Pooled approach differences unclear; possible overlapping cohorts need checking; FT challenge/rate limit Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Outcomes of Nonsurgical Treatments for Symptomatic Adult Degenerative Scoliosis: A Systematic Review.
sources.population: Symptomatic adult degenerative scoliosis, age at least 50, nonsurgical interventions
sources.findings: Schoutens et al., 2020 (online 2019) systematic review. DOI 10.1093/pm/pnz253, PMID 31617915. Abstract; institutional FT PDF located but direct fetch 403. Symptomatic degenerative scoliosis ≥50, nonsurgical interventions, follow-up ≥6 weeks; six studies. Injection evidence low; yoga/bracing very low; no specific PT evidence found in review period. Cannot advise for/against these approaches from available evidence. This is uncertainty, not a contraindication against exercise. No condition-specific ordinary-training load/ROM ban supported.
sources.limitations: Low injection and very-low yoga/bracing certainty; no specific PT evidence in search period; absence is not an exercise contraindication Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Conservative Treatment in Adult Degenerative Scoliosis: a Prospective Cohort Study.
sources.population: Nonsurgical thoracolumbar adult degenerative scoliosis
sources.findings: Bayram et al., 2024 prospective uncontrolled cohort. DOI 10.26574/maedica.2024.19.1.23, PMID 38736938, FT PMC11079735. FT. Forty nonsurgical thoracolumbar ADS participants enrolled, 30 women completed. Combined modalities (heat/TENS/ultrasound) plus stretching, strengthening, stabilization, posture/balance/coordination, 15 sessions/3 weeks, 60 min/day five days/week. Methods p. 25 says one patient continued a home program; Discussion p. 27 reports patients continuing one hour/day at least three days/week. These participation descriptions conflict and remain unresolved. The Discussion schedule is reported home prescription, not measured adherence; actual home participation/adherence was not established. Pain/disability/QoL improved at 1/3 months. No control, ten dropouts, multiple cointerventions; no causal exercise-specific effect or long-term curve effect established. Detailed adverse-event surveillance not identified; health problems among attrition reasons cannot be assigned to treatment. Not a proof that every listed exercise is safe for all curves.
sources.limitations: Ten dropouts, no control, multiple modalities; cannot identify exercise-specific or long-term curve effect Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Serial case reporting yoga for idiopathic and degenerative scoliosis.
sources.population: Mixed idiopathic/degenerative scoliosis, curves 6–120 degrees; degenerative subgroup details not extracted
sources.findings: Fishman et al., 2014 case series. DOI 10.7453/gahmj.2013.064, PMID 25568820, PMC4268609. Abstract and available methods/results snippets; FT browser challenged. Twenty-five mixed idiopathic/degenerative scoliosis cases, curves 6–120°, side plank with convex side down, daily practice, average follow-up 6.8 months. Curve reductions reported among adherers; no randomized/control group, mixed age/etiology and adherence selection. No defensible universal one-sided plank prescription, side assignment or curve-correction promise. Actual degenerative subgroup/adverse details require full extraction before considering a therapeutic mapping.
sources.limitations: Mixed ages/etiology, adherence selection; convex-side-down description cannot authorize universal side assignment Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Adults with idiopathic scoliosis improve disability after motor and cognitive rehabilitation: results of a randomised controlled trial.
sources.population: Adult idiopathic scoliosis, lower progression risk, main curve under 35 degrees
sources.findings: Monticone et al., 2016 RCT, deliberately indirect. DOI 10.1007/s00586-016-4528-y, PMID 27015689. Abstract. 130 adults with idiopathic, lower-progression-risk scoliosis, main curve <35°; 20-week active self-correction/task exercises/CBT versus general mobilization/stretching/strengthening. Favorable disability outcome described, but this is not a degenerative-scoliosis RCT. Do not transfer its curve threshold, dose, side-specific correction or outcomes into ADS as direct evidence. Full harms unavailable.
sources.limitations: Idiopathic rather than degenerative disease; do not transfer threshold/dose/curve correction as direct ADS evidence Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.title: Adult degenerative scoliosis: challenges in diagnosis, pain management, and surgical decision-making.
sources.population: Adult degenerative scoliosis, varied curve/symptom/comorbidity patterns
sources.findings: Zhao et al., 2026 narrative review (not guideline). DOI 10.3389/fsurg.2026.1807406, PMID 42518838, publisher text. Relevant text inspected. Discusses individualized rehabilitation by curve pattern, balance, stenosis phenotype/comorbidity; high-quality protocol trials still needed. This is background/expert synthesis, not direct proof of extensor strengthening or cycling for every ADS patient and not a current final exercise CPG.
sources.limitations: Background/expert synthesis; high-quality protocol trials still required Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.findings: Active rehabilitation recommended; optimal exercise mode, intensity and dose remain uncertain.
sources.limitations: Full-thickness tears and repair protocols are separate applicability states.

sources.findings: Motor control slightly favored disability short term SMD −0.29 and medium term −0.33; pain superiority unclear.
sources.limitations: Relative-program benefit does not demonstrate alternative exercises harmful.

sources.population: Adults 18–65, symptoms ≥3 months, ultrasound tendinopathy; full-thickness tear, elevation <90°, resting pain >40/100 excluded.
sources.findings: DASH group difference −1.37 (95% CI −6.72 to 3.99); no high-load superiority.
sources.limitations: Eligibility exclusions are not contraindications; regimen is study extraction, not app prescription.

sources.population: Adults with rotator cuff tendinopathy.
sources.findings: Shoulder exercise may help versus no treatment; most adjunct superiority unclear.

sources.title: Management of Rotator Cuff Injuries: Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline
sources.population: Small/medium symptomatic full-thickness tears; separate large/massive/unrepairable and postoperative topics.
sources.findings: Both PT and repair improve patient outcomes; nonoperative tear size/atrophy/fatty infiltration may progress over 5–10 years.
sources.limitations: Early/delayed repair mobilization evidence is not unrestricted resistance clearance.

sources.title: Effectiveness of physical therapy in treating atraumatic full-thickness rotator cuff tears: a multicenter prospective cohort study
sources.population: Symptomatic MRI-confirmed atraumatic full-thickness tears, age 18–100; injury-related presentation/prior surgery/GHOA/capsulitis excluded.
sources.findings: Approximately 75% avoided surgery at two years; patient outcomes improved.
sources.limitations: Not acute traumatic tears, repairs or combined-pathology clearance.

sources.title: The Predictors of Surgery for Symptomatic, Atraumatic Full-Thickness Rotator Cuff Tears Change Over Time: Ten-Year Outcomes of the MOON Shoulder Prospective Cohort
sources.population: Symptomatic atraumatic full-thickness tears.
sources.findings: Nonoperated patient-reported outcomes improved and remained stable; surgery predictors changed over time.
sources.limitations: Cannot establish structural healing or exercise-specific safety.

sources.title: Fifteen-Year Results of a Comparative Analysis of Tendon Repair Versus Physiotherapy for Small-to-Medium-Sized Rotator Cuff Tears: A Concise Follow-up of Previous Reports
sources.population: Full-thickness tears ≤3 cm; gradual-onset and minor-trauma acute-on-chronic presentations.
sources.findings: Repair favored Constant by 11.8 and ASES by 13.9 points; 15/51 PT crossed to surgery. In 26 unrepaired tears AP size increased 16.2→31.6 mm.
sources.limitations: Long-term functional conflict with nonoperative cohort must remain; no universal load cap.

sources.title: Clinical Practice Guidelines for Diagnosis and Non-Surgical Treatment of Primary Frozen Shoulder
sources.population: Adults with primary frozen shoulder.
sources.findings: Isolated self-stretch evidence insufficient; strengthening recommendation clinician discretion, very-low certainty; pooled pain MD −1.02, I² 97%.
sources.limitations: Secondary/postsurgical stiffness not interchangeable with primary frozen shoulder.

sources.title: Shoulder Pain and Mobility Deficits: Adhesive Capsulitis
sources.population: Adhesive capsulitis assessed by pain, mobility and tissue irritability.
sources.findings: Recommends functional pain-free ROM and stretching intensity matched to tissue irritability.
sources.limitations: No automatic app diagnosis or universal hold-time progression.

sources.title: Gentle thawing of the frozen shoulder: a prospective study of supervised neglect versus intensive physical therapy in seventy-seven patients with frozen shoulder syndrome followed up for two years
sources.population: 77 idiopathic frozen shoulders; >50% GH restriction ≥3 months.
sources.findings: Constant ≥80 at 24 months: 89% versus 63%, favoring pain-limited group.
sources.limitations: Not all secondary/postoperative cases or all stages.

sources.title: Effect of rotator cuff strengthening as an adjunct to standard care in subjects with adhesive capsulitis: A randomized controlled trial
sources.population: Adhesive capsulitis; stage and exact execution not established by inspected abstract.
sources.findings: SPADI favored added strengthening; abstract reports improved pain/ROM/function after 12 sessions within four weeks.
sources.limitations: No exact exercise mapping or painful end-range rule follows.

sources.title: Management of adults with primary frozen shoulder in secondary care (UK FROST): a multicentre, pragmatic, three-arm, superiority randomised clinical trial
sources.population: Secondary-care primary frozen shoulder.
sources.findings: No clinically important superior treatment at 12 months; packages differed.
sources.limitations: No claim all patients recover without reassessment.

sources.title: Physical Therapist Management of Glenohumeral Joint Osteoarthritis: A Clinical Practice Guideline from the American Physical Therapy Association
sources.population: Adults with native GHOA and anatomic TSA; not reverse/revision arthroplasty or primary RA.
sources.findings: PT may benefit selected patients; no specific intervention superiority established.
sources.limitations: Hip/knee OA or postoperative data cannot supply native-shoulder exercise efficacy.

sources.title: Three-Year Follow-up of Conservative Treatments of Shoulder Osteoarthritis in Older Patients
sources.population: Chinese adults >65 with unilateral shoulder OA.
sources.findings: Pain/function/quality-of-life generally improved at three years, with changing intermediate trajectories.
sources.limitations: No exact exercises/dose or general safety clearance.

sources.title: Effectiveness of nonoperative treatment in patients with glenohumeral osteoarthritis: a prospective cohort study
sources.population: Primary GHOA; prior surgery/fracture/dislocation/full-thickness tear excluded.
sources.findings: No ASES change difference with PT (P=.524); 31% met clinical improvement; 14/62 underwent TSA.
sources.limitations: No causal conclusion strengthening harmful or no patient can benefit.

sources.title: BESS/BOA patient care pathways: Atraumatic shoulder instability
sources.population: Atraumatic instability with laxity/motor-control and possible microtrauma structural components.
sources.findings: Physiotherapy first-line; evidence limited, persistent complex displacement needs specialist assessment.
sources.limitations: Atraumatic presentation is not equivalent to acute traumatic anterior instability.

sources.title: British Elbow and Shoulder Society practice guidelines: Rehabilitation following traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation (post-operative and non-operative care)
sources.population: Traumatic anterior dislocation, separate postoperative/nonoperative pathways.
sources.findings: Aligned phased pathways with protection, early movement/strength, progressive strength and return-to-function criteria.
sources.limitations: No exact sling, ROM or exercise load rule extracted from abstract.

sources.title: Exercise for multidirectional instability of the shoulder
sources.population: Multidirectional instability, traumatic or nontraumatic in review eligibility.
sources.findings: No eligible randomized evidence; benefits and harms uncertain for the review question.
sources.limitations: Review eligibility differs from relative-program questions; comparison explanation is interpretation, not verified excluded-study rationale.

sources.title: Comparison of 2 Exercise Rehabilitation Programs for Multidirectional Instability of the Glenohumeral Joint: A Randomized Controlled Trial
sources.population: Age 12–35, nontraumatic/nonstructural MDI, MRI exclusion of structural lesions.
sources.findings: At 24 weeks WOSI difference 12.6, MISS 15.4, pain −2.0 favored Watson; no meaningful difference demonstrated for dislocation incidence.
sources.limitations: Not traumatic structural instability, repair or unrestricted gym clearance.

sources.title: Acute rehabilitation following traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation (ARTISAN): pragmatic, multicentre, randomised controlled trial
sources.population: First-time radiologically confirmed anterior traumatic dislocation, mean age45, managed nonoperatively; neurovascular complications/bilateral injury/surgical candidates excluded.
sources.findings: Six-month Oxford instability difference 1.5 (95% CI −0.3 to 3.5), no worthwhile extra-PT superiority; similar complications, ten redislocations overall.
sources.limitations: Not no rehabilitation, recurrent structural instability or immediate unrestricted return.

sources.title: Shoulder Pain Diagnosis, Treatment and Referral Guidelines for Primary, Community and Intermediate Care
sources.population: Adults presenting with shoulder pain; condition-specific pathways distinct.
sources.findings: Conservative-care context; no exact AC exercise regimen extracted.
sources.limitations: No exact dose or pressing ban follows from pathway context.

sources.title: Current evidence for nonpharmacological interventions and criteria for surgical management of persistent acromioclavicular joint osteoarthritis: A systematic review
sources.population: Isolated clinical/radiological AC OA ≥3 months, age≥16.
sources.findings: No evidence for individual/combined nonpharmacologic effectiveness in included studies.
sources.limitations: Do not turn failure windows into app progression rules.

sources.title: A systematic review of the treatment of primary acromioclavicular joint osteoarthritis
sources.population: Clinical/radiological primary AC OA; some concomitant cuff/impingement pathology.
sources.findings: Positive within-study changes; heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis; PT evidence sparse.
sources.limitations: Surgery and injection improvements cannot prescribe a particular strengthening/stretch dose.

sources.title: Manual Physical Therapy for Injection-Confirmed Nonacute Acromioclavicular Joint Pain
sources.population: Injection-confirmed nonacute AC pain, mean41,85%male, military setting; four normal radiographs.
sources.findings: SPADI improved25.9 points at4weeks/29.8 at6months; not isolated exercise efficacy.
sources.limitations: Study delaying strength to4weeks does not establish early-strength contraindication.

sources.title: Management of acromioclavicular joint disease by manual therapy versus corticosteroid injections: the protocol of a non-inferiority study
sources.population: Radiographic symptomatic AC OA age40–70, symptoms>3months.
sources.findings: Planned activity-pain endpoint, no outcome results extracted.
sources.limitations: No workout restriction, benefit or noninferiority inferred.

sources.title: No differences between conservative and surgical management of acromioclavicular joint osteoarthritis: a scoping review
sources.population: Primary/post-traumatic OA and distal-clavicle osteolysis mixed.
sources.findings: All reports improved; no superiority/equivalence established.
sources.limitations: Do not transplant distal-clavicle osteolysis or traumatic-separation rules to primary OA.

sources.title: Lateral Elbow Pain and Muscle Function Impairments
sources.population: Subacute/chronic lateral elbow tendinopathy; not medial disease or acute rupture
sources.findings: Grade B resisted wrist-extensor exercise; grade F phased return to high-demand activity; synthesis suggests 3×15 for 6–12 weeks but no validated load/progression.
sources.limitations: Population: lateral elbow pain/tendinopathy; exercise recommendation specifically subacute/chronic LET. Grade B supports resisted wrist-extensor exercise using isometric, concentric and/or eccentric contractions. Suggested synthesis dose: 3 sets of 15 repetitions over 6–12 weeks; load/progression determination is inadequately described. Phased return to demanding work/sport is expert-opinion grade F. Stretching alone lacks convincing durable advantage; combinations cannot isolate stretching effects. Guideline acknowledges limited specific return-to-function information. Candidate wrist-extensor loading can therefore be researched, but there is no validated app-wide kilogram ceiling, elbow-angle ceiling or mandatory eccentric-only sequence. Harms/progression cannot be assumed absent or standardized.

sources.title: A randomized controlled trial of eccentric vs. concentric graded exercise in chronic tennis elbow (lateral elbow tendinopathy)
sources.population: Adults with tennis elbow >3 months
sources.findings: Approximately 10% higher pain responder rate (reported NNT 10) and strength advantage for eccentric group; no function/QOL difference.
sources.limitations: 120 adults with tennis elbow >3 months randomized 60/60 to daily home eccentric lowering versus concentric lifting with gradually increased load for 3 months. Evaluations at 1, 2, 3, 6 and 12 months. Eccentrics produced faster pain improvement (approximately 10% greater responder rate; reported NNT 10) and larger strength improvement; function and quality of life did not differ. Abstract verifies daily frequency and intervention duration, not exact set/repetition, starting weight or progression increment; those values must not be copied from a tertiary account. Harms not reported in the inspected abstract. This supports a loading candidate for chronic LET, not proof that concentric lifting is contraindicated or evidence about medial elbow disease.

sources.title: Manual therapy and exercise for lateral elbow pain
sources.population: Adults with lateral elbow pain, mean trial ages 38–52
sources.findings: Low-certainty end-treatment pain difference −0.53/10 (95% CI −0.92 to −0.14), disability −5/100 (−9.22 to −0.77); effects not sustained.
sources.limitations: 23 trials/1,612 adults; heterogeneous manual therapy, exercise or combinations. Against minimal/no intervention, low-certainty evidence at 4 weeks–3 months favored treatment by 0.53/10 pain points (95% CI 0.14–0.92) and 5/100 disability points (0.77–9.22). Benefits were not sustained; multimodal pooling cannot identify the best exercise or dose. Adverse events were uncertain, often mild/transient pain or bruising; no serious events reported in included reporting, but incomplete ascertainment prevents declaring universal safety. Compared with minimal treatment, event RR 3.69 had a wide CI (0.98–13.97). This moderates the older CPG's confidence: therapeutic loading is a candidate, with modest/uncertain incremental benefit rather than assured rehabilitation efficacy.

sources.title: Position statement: nonoperative management of lateral epicondylitis in adults
sources.population: Adults >18 with lateral epicondylitis; 9 exercise studies/673 randomized patients
sources.findings: Similar pain/function through one year; recommendation does not support exercise physiotherapy superiority.
sources.limitations: Exercise/strengthening versus no active treatment included 9 studies/673 randomized adults. Through 1 year, pooled pain/function outcomes were similar; recommendation did not support exercise-based physiotherapy as superior. Different comparators, inclusion criteria and multimodal grouping explain why this cannot be silently merged with LET-G1 as unanimous support. No exercise-specific harm inference follows from lack of superiority. No universal exercise prohibition is justified.

sources.title: Eccentric exercise therapy for medial epicondylitis: A systematic review of clinical outcomes
sources.population: Medial flexor-pronator origin tendinopathy
sources.findings: Within-group pain/function improvement; one RCT superiority; other comparisons unclear; low overall certainty, no pooling.
sources.limitations: Search through January 2025; five clinical studies/143 patients receiving wrist flexor-pronator eccentric loading, including randomized, pre/post and comparative designs. Within-group pain/function improvements were frequent; one RCT showed between-group superiority, others did not. One uncontrolled 11-year report suggested persistence. Heterogeneity and small samples precluded pooling; authors rate overall certainty low. Abstract does not establish exact protocols, harms or a validated exercise restriction. Newer synthesis prevents claiming that no medial-specific research exists, while still leaving a weak evidence base.

sources.title: Clinical outcomes of the addition of eccentrics for rehabilitation of previously failed treatments of golfers elbow
sources.population: Chronic medial epicondylosis after failed prior treatment, mean age49, 13 men/7 women
sources.findings: DASH 34.7→7.9; sports DASH 73.9→13.2; attribution to eccentric component impossible.
sources.limitations: 20 patients (13 male/7 female, mean 49 years) with chronic medial epicondylosis after unsuccessful prior treatment. Added rubber-bar eccentric wrist-flexor release to stretching, ultrasound, massage and heat/ice; no control group. Abstract reports 3×15 twice daily, while discussion says daily: internal frequency inconsistency is unresolved. Mean treatment 6.1 weeks; DASH 34.7→7.9 and sport-DASH 73.9→13.2. Improvement cannot isolate eccentrics or exclude natural history/expectation. Adverse-event ascertainment is not adequately reported. The text's flexor/extensor wording in a figure caption is inconsistent with the stated wrist-flexor intervention; do not build execution solely from that caption.

sources.title: Tendinopathies Around the Elbow Part 2: Medial Elbow, Distal Biceps and Triceps Tendinopathies
sources.population: Medial elbow, distal biceps and triceps discussed separately
sources.findings: Sparse higher-level evidence; differential includes ulnar neuropathy/ligament pathology; activity modification is clinical advice.
sources.limitations: Review addresses medial elbow, distal biceps and triceps separately; notes sparse high-level evidence and supports conservative management before surgery in appropriate presentations. This is context/expert interpretation, not an RCT defining allowable wrist flexion/pronation, valgus load or pulling volume. Medial pain can coexist with ulnar neuropathy and ligament pathology; diagnosis-specific evidence must remain separate. No dose or universal contraindication is extracted from this source.

sources.title: Clinical outcomes following treatment of distal biceps tendon partial tears and tendinopathy: a systematic review
sources.population: 114 tendinopathies and 500 partial tears; diagnosis and treatment selection heterogeneous.
sources.findings: Both strategies described improvement; heterogeneous low-level evidence prevents pooling/equivalence inference.
sources.limitations: 30 studies/614 patients: 114 tendinopathies and 500 partial tears; no level I/II comparative studies, so no meta-analysis. Both operative and nonoperative reports describe pain/function improvement, but selection strongly favors nonoperative care for tendinopathy and surgery for tears. Conservative care varies (activity modification, immobilization, strengthening); dose reporting is poor. These mixed-pathology results cannot establish a loading protocol or rupture risk for isolated tendinopathy. Tendinopathy/partial tear/complete rupture and postoperative rehabilitation must remain distinct. Low-level literature and heterogeneity, rather than evidence of equivalence, constrain comparisons.

sources.title: Multifaceted Exercise Prescription in the Management of an Overhead Athlete with Suspected Distal Biceps Tendinopathy: A Case Report
sources.population: 19-year-old male collegiate pitcher, suspected distal biceps tendinopathy, symptoms6 weeks; no imaging confirmation
sources.findings: Pain/function/strength improved; returned to offseason pitching; component efficacy cannot be isolated.
sources.limitations: One 19-year-old baseball pitcher with suspected distal biceps tendinopathy, symptoms 6 weeks, five visits over 4 weeks. Pain-free ROM, manual therapy, forearm stretching and eccentric loading progressed to concentric and sport-specific plyometrics. Narrative prescribes eccentric 3×7, daily after visit two, controlled 3-second lowering; first-visit table instead lists 3×10 with 3-lb dumbbell. Stretch 3×30 seconds; later concentric 3×10. This case-specific/table discrepancy precludes one canonical dose. Improved pain/function/strength and returned to offseason pitching; no comparator and diagnosis not imaging-confirmed. Avoiding provoking heavy lifting, power cleans and pitching was individualized treatment advice, not tested universal contraindications. Harms not systematically established.

sources.title: A Case Series of Symptomatic Distal Biceps Tendinopathy
sources.population: 12 tendinopathies and 9 partial tears; complete ruptures excluded.
sources.findings: Five continued failures undergoing surgery had partial tears; no isolated exercise effect.
sources.limitations: 21 patients, 12 tendinopathy and 9 partial tears. Complete ruptures were excluded and managed surgically. Initial care included a long-arm splint in forearm supination for 3 weeks, NSAIDs/physical therapy; refractory cases proceeded to ultrasound-guided injection and, for five continued failures with partial tears, surgery. No exercise-versus-control test or isolated exercise dose. Splint position is an initial treatment exposure, not a safe workout ROM threshold. Mixed pathology and escalation confound attribution; report cannot prove which movements cause rupture.

sources.title: Management of Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline
sources.population: Adults with CTS
sources.findings: AAOS 2024 long-term nonoperative-treatment option rates evidence quality High and option strength Limited (Downgraded) after Evidence-to-Decision deliberation. Exercise and listed modalities do not improve long-term patient-reported outcomes; this is not proof of short-term harm.
sources.limitations: High evidence quality and downgraded Limited option strength are different axes. The long-term statement does not establish short-term inefficacy/harm, an individual exercise protocol, or a universal wrist-load/angle prohibition.

sources.title: Hand Pain and Sensory Deficits: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: Revision 2026
sources.population: Nonsurgical mild–moderate CTS, no thenar atrophy, normal two-point discrimination
sources.findings: GradeC optional combined orthotic/stretching; monitor meaningful improvement; no new therapeutic-exercise evidence in updated section.
sources.limitations: Grade C retains optional combined orthotic/stretching treatment for **nonsurgical mild–moderate CTS without thenar atrophy and with normal two-point discrimination**; monitor meaningful improvement. It explicitly found no new therapeutic-exercise evidence for this section. A limited selected-population option and AAOS's long-term negative finding are different questions, not proof of universal gliding efficacy. Exact stretching execution/dose needs the underlying trial; the guideline recommendation alone is insufficient. No general gym-position ceiling is given.

sources.title: Effectiveness of Tendon and Nerve Gliding Exercises in the Treatment of Patients With Mild Idiopathic Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: A Randomized Controlled Trial
sources.population: Mild idiopathic CTS,13 men/67 women among completers
sources.findings: No between-group symptom/function/grip/pinch advantage; within-group gains cannot prove added benefit.
sources.limitations: 80 mild idiopathic CTS patients completed splint+median nerve/tendon glides versus splint alone over 6 weeks. Splints at night, daytime as needed. No significant between-group difference in symptom/function scores, grip or pinch; within-group improvement cannot establish added glide benefit. AAOS evidence appendix reports exercise 3 times/day, 10 repetitions, each position held 5 seconds; dose is secondary extraction, not independently verified methods. Harms not established by the accessible abstract. This is a limited glide candidate, not default treatment for severe CTS, another nerve diagnosis, or postoperative CTS.
sources.executionNote: The follow-up review inspected the full trial methods and Figure 2a–e. The five numbered hand positions return to fully open fingers between shapes. Adding glides to the splint did not show a significant between-group advantage in this trial.

sources.title: The Comparative Effectiveness of Combined Lumbrical Muscle Splints and Stretches on Symptoms and Function in Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
sources.population: 124 volunteers with mild to moderate CTS; narrower analyzed-population details come from cts-g3.
sources.findings: Primary abstract: significant time effects at four, twelve and twenty-four weeks; CTQ-Function/DASH interaction at twelve weeks, with post hoc differences for lumbrical-splint/general-stretch and cock-up-splint/lumbrical-stretch combinations versus the other two groups. At twenty-four weeks, a significantly greater percentage with cock-up splint plus lumbrical-intensive stretch achieved clinically important CTQ-Function improvement. Surgery elected by 25.5% by twenty-four weeks. Exact effect sizes, p-values and responder denominators are not supplied in the abstract.
sources.limitations: Full primary methods unavailable. Six-times-daily stretching is explicit, while exact geometry, repetitions, hold, load, progression and stopping rules remain unknown. Preserve the primary twenty-four-week responder advantage alongside the secondary guideline no-superiority summary; do not invent numerical significance/effect size or isolate stretching benefit.

sources.title: Correlation of Segmental Carpal Tunnel Pressures with Changes in Hand and Wrist Positions in Patients with Carpal Tunnel Syndrome and Controls
sources.population: 39 CTS patients/12 controls
sources.findings: Pressure varies by position,grip,location; relaxed neutral generally lower,extension often higher; no clinical safe angle measured.
sources.limitations: Mechanistic surrogate; not outcome evidence for a universal wrist-extension prohibition. [Primary abstract](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1016/S0266-7681%2898%2980009-0). DOI 10.1016/S0266-7681(98)80009-0. 39 CTS patients/12 controls; measured pressure at 1-cm intervals in relaxed/gripping hands across neutral/flexed/extended wrists. Patient pressures exceeded controls; relaxed neutral generally lower, extension often higher than flexion. Position, grip and measurement location interacted; simple universal pressure rules are inappropriate. Mechanistic study, no workout intervention, clinical follow-up or safe angle/load endpoint. Supports exploring a symptom-tolerable wrist position, not declaring all loaded wrist extension harmful.

sources.title: Hand Pain and Sensory Deficits: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
sources.population: Nonsurgical mild–moderate CTS, no thenar atrophy, normal two-point discrimination
sources.findings: 2019 CPG secondary Baker extraction: 103 analyzed, normal two-point discrimination/no thenar atrophy. It describes twelve-week differences and no three-way interaction at four/twenty-four weeks, then summarizes no superior intervention; 25.5% surgery by twenty-four weeks without group difference. Primary abstract cts-p2 instead reports a twenty-four-week clinically important functional-response advantage for cock-up splint plus lumbrical-intensive stretches. Different endpoint/account summaries remain unresolved.
sources.limitations: Secondary extraction independently re-read at CPG50. No control arm isolates stretching. Exact stretch holds/range/progression remain unknown; orthosis joint angles are not stretch geometry.
